summary: Describes version 4 of the TCP convergence layer for delay-tolerant networking. It carries bundles of Bundle Protocol version 7 reliably over TCP, and resolves implementation issues found in version 3 from RFC 7242. It also includes security and extensibility mechanisms.

plainLanguage.summary: A delivery truck for bundles that uses the ordinary reliable TCP roads to carry them from one stop to the next.

questions: how to send bundle protocol over tcp
how does dtn carry bundles over tcp
what is the tcpcl contact header
subtitle: How delay-tolerant networking nodes carry bundles to each other over ordinary TCP, with optional TLS security.

tldr.problem: Delay-tolerant networks move data in bundles through stressed, intermittent links, and each hop needs a convergence layer that carries bundles over some native protocol. Bundle Protocol version 7 needed such a layer for TCP, and version 3 of it (RFC 7242) had implementation issues.
tldr.mechanism: TCPCLv4 opens a TCP connection, exchanges a fixed-length Contact Header, optionally runs a TLS handshake, then negotiates session parameters with SESS_INIT. Bundles are then sent as numbered transfers split into XFER_SEGMENT messages and acknowledged with XFER_ACK.
tldr.outcome: It gives BPv7 reliable bundle transport between adjacent nodes, with TLS authentication of node IDs, extension points, and a clean session termination procedure. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Keepalive guidance
facts.value: No shorter than 30 s on shared networks, no longer than 600 s

today: RFC 9174 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2022. It resolves implementation issues in the earlier TCPCL version 3 from RFC 7242 and has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) is an end-to-end architecture for communication in highly stressed environments, including those with intermittent connectivity, long or variable delays, and high bit error rates. The Bundle Protocol version 7 (BPv7, RFC 9171) builds a store-and-forward overlay network and needs a convergence-layer adapter to send and receive bundles over some native protocol. This document defines one that uses TCP, called TCPCLv4.

Both BP and the TCPCL sit at the application layer of the Internet model, with optional TLS and TCP below them. The TCPCL only moves bundles between adjacent entities. It does not define bundle formats, how peers are found, how bundles are routed, or how certificates are issued.
sections.plainLanguage: Bundles are parcels that may have to wait at many stops on a long, bumpy trip. This protocol is the part that carries a parcel from one stop to the next stop using the normal reliable TCP roads.

sections.title: Entities, Sessions and Transfer Streams
sections.content:
A TCPCL entity starts sessions actively and may also listen passively. A session lives inside exactly one TCP connection and ends when that connection ends. Inside a session there are two transfer streams, one in each direction, and they do not logically interact. After setup the protocol is symmetric: both sides can send bundles at once.

Session parameters are fixed once negotiated. To use different parameters, a new session must be established. The RFC assumes that opening a TCP connection is cheap compared with the size of the transfers.

Within one stream, transfers are serialized and segments from different bundles are never interleaved. The RFC notes that this causes head-of-queue blocking, and suggests BP-layer fragmentation or several sessions between the same peers when interleaving is wanted. It also describes session-keeping policies (persistent, ephemeral, and active-only polling) and segmentation policies as administration choices.

Persistent session
Keep one session open with KEEPALIVEs. Fewer setups, but wasted resources when idle.
Ephemeral sessions
Open a session only when something must be sent. Pays TCP and TLS setup each time.
Active-only polling
For entities that cannot accept incoming connections. Less efficient than as-needed sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: A session is one phone call between two depots, and each call has two one-way lanes for parcels. If you want different call rules, you hang up and call again.

sections.title: Contact Header and Session Setup
sections.content:
The entity that opens the TCP connection is the active entity. Destination port 4556 is the registered TCPCL port, though others may be configured. As soon as the connection is up, the active entity sends its Contact Header; the passive entity waits for it and then replies with its own. A waiting entity should time out after no more than one minute (60 seconds). Retries after a failed connection SHOULD use binary exponential backoff, capped at about one minute.

The Contact Header is fixed length: the four-octet magic dtn! (0x64 0x74 0x6E 0x21), a one-octet Version of 4, and a one-octet Flags field. The only defined flag is CAN_TLS (0x01). If the magic string is wrong the connection MUST be terminated. The active entity sends its highest supported version first; a passive entity that does not support it replies with its Contact Header and then terminates with reason code Version mismatch.

Whether TLS is used is the logical AND of the two CAN_TLS flags, then checked against local policy. The RECOMMENDED policy is to require TLS for every session, even without authentication. After the headers, the active entity sends SESS_INIT carrying a Keepalive Interval (16 bits), Segment MRU (64 bits), Transfer MRU (64 bits), the sender's node ID and any session extension items. The negotiated keepalive is the minimum of the two intervals, and zero disables KEEPALIVEs. An unacceptable MRU or interval means termination with reason code Contact Failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The two depots first show each other a secret handshake card that says 'dtn!' and the rulebook version they speak. Then they agree how big each box piece can be and how often to say 'still here'.

sections.title: TLS and Node Authentication
sections.content:
When TLS is negotiated, the handshake starts right after the Contact Header exchange and before any other TCPCL message. The active entity takes the TLS client role. Entities SHALL follow BCP 195 (RFC 7525) and use TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) or a compatible successor. The passive entity SHALL supply a certificate and request one from the client, so authentication goes in both directions. Once TLS is up, there is no way to downgrade the session to non-TLS.

A certificate can identify an entity in three ways, in priority order: a NODE-ID (a subjectAltName otherName of type BundleEID holding the node ID), a DNS name, or a network address. The ideal is the node ID, because DTN node addresses can change over time. Certificates must follow the PKIX profile of RFC 5280 and be version 3. A new extended key usage, id-kp-bundleSecurity, marks keys trusted to act as bundle nodes.

Authentication runs in phases: certification path validation (with optional OCSP), network-level checks (DNS-ID and IP address) and, just before parameter negotiation, NODE-ID validation against the node ID in SESS_INIT. A failed check where policy requires success ends the session with Contact Failure. The recommended policy enables OCSP, requires the bundleSecurity EKU if an EKU is present, and requires a validated node ID.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS is like both drivers showing photo ID that a trusted office has stamped. The best ID names the exact depot, not just the street it sits on.

sections.title: Transferring Bundles
sections.content:
Each bundle is one transfer with a 64-bit Transfer ID chosen by the sender. The sender splits it into XFER_SEGMENT messages no larger than the receiver's Segment MRU. The first has the START flag (0x02), the last has END (0x01), and a single-segment transfer has both. Transfer IDs start at zero and increase by one unless another scheme is used.

For every segment, the receiver SHALL answer with an XFER_ACK whose acknowledged length is the running total of data received. For example, segments of 100, 200, 500 and 1000 octets are acknowledged with lengths 100, 300, 800 and 1800. The sender SHOULD send further segments without waiting for acknowledgments, which is pipelining. The acknowledgments let a sender resume with reactive fragmentation after an interruption.

A receiver may send XFER_REFUSE at any time after a segment arrives, with a reason code. The sender must finish the segment in flight, because a message cannot be cut short, and must send no more segments of that bundle. An optional Transfer Length extension, sent in the START segment, announces the total size so a receiver can refuse early or prepare storage; if the actual size differs, the receiver refuses with Not Acceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: A big parcel is sent in pieces, and the receiver says 'got this much so far' after each piece. If the receiver already has the parcel, it shouts 'stop, I have it' and the sender quits.

sections.title: Messages and Extension Items
sections.content:
After the Contact Header and any TLS handshake, every message starts with a one-octet Message Type. All integers are sent in network byte order and the old variable-length SDNV encoding of version 3 is gone. SESS_INIT, SESS_TERM, XFER_SEGMENT, XFER_ACK, XFER_REFUSE, KEEPALIVE and MSG_REJECT are the seven message types. A receiver that sees an unknown type sends MSG_REJECT with reason Message Type Unknown and closes the TCP connection; the other reasons are Message Unsupported and Message Unexpected.

Extensibility comes from session extension items (in SESS_INIT) and transfer extension items (in the START segment of a transfer). Both use a type-length-value container with a one-octet flags field, a 16-bit type and a 16-bit length. If the CRITICAL flag (0x01) is set on an unknown item, the session is terminated (session items) or the transfer is refused with Extension Failure (transfer items). Unknown non-critical items are skipped. The only extension defined here is the Transfer Length Extension, type 0x0001.
sections.plainLanguage: Every note the depots pass starts with a label saying what kind of note it is. Extra stickers can be added, and if a sticker is marked 'must understand' and you do not, you refuse the job.

sections.title: Keepalives and Session Termination
sections.content:
KEEPALIVE is a one-octet message with no data. Each side sends one whenever the negotiated interval passes with no message sent. Entities SHOULD choose an interval no shorter than 30 seconds on shared networks and no longer than 10 minutes (600 seconds). If nothing is received for an implementation-defined time, the entity terminates with reason Idle timeout; that time SHOULD be twice the interval.

To end a session cleanly, one side sends SESS_TERM with the REPLY flag at 0, and the other answers with a matching SESS_TERM with REPLY set to 1. After sending SESS_TERM the session is Ending: in-progress transfers may finish, but no new transfer may start or be accepted, and new attempts get XFER_REFUSE with Session Terminating. SESS_TERM reason codes are Unknown, Idle timeout, Version mismatch, Busy, Contact Failure and Resource Exhaustion. An entity in a hurry MAY close the TCP connection immediately after sending SESS_TERM, ideally acknowledging received segments first.
sections.plainLanguage: While nothing is being delivered, the depots whisper 'still here' every so often. To finish, one says goodbye, the other says goodbye back, and parcels already on the way are allowed to arrive.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC organizes threats using BCP 72. Without TLS, node IDs, configuration data and all bundle data are visible to passive eavesdroppers, so it advises always using TLS even when authentication is unavailable. TCPCL protects a single hop only; it does not protect data at rest or give end-to-end security, which is the job of the bundle security mechanisms in RFC 9172.

Other threats covered include version downgrade, TLS stripping (an on-path attacker clearing CAN_TLS, so policy should disallow non-TLS sessions where TLS is available), weak cipher suites, incomplete certificate chains, certificate validation bugs, impersonating a node ID, and denial of service. A "data dribble" attack uses a tiny Segment MRU to bury data in overhead. Defenses include rejecting unacceptable MRUs or keepalive intervals during negotiation. Transfer IDs are predictable by design, which the RFC says gives an attacker no benefit. TLS is mandatory to implement but optional to use.
sections.plainLanguage: Without a locked truck, anyone watching the road can see the parcels. So the rules say to lock the truck every time and to check the driver's ID.

messages.label: XFER_SEGMENT (start)
messages.note: First of three segments of lengths L1, L2 and L3.

items.label: Unknown
items.desc: The reason for refusal is unknown or not specified.

items.label: Completed
items.desc: The receiver already has the complete bundle.

items.label: No Resources
items.desc: The receiver's resources are exhausted; sender should fragment reactively before retrying.

items.label: Retransmit
items.desc: The bundle must be retransmitted in its entirety.

items.label: Not Acceptable
items.desc: A problem with the bundle data or transfer extension data; do not retry the same bundle with the same extensions.

items.label: Extension Failure
items.desc: A failure processing the Transfer Extension Items.

items.label: Session Terminating
items.desc: The receiver is terminating the session; retry later in a different session.

items.label: XFER_ACK
items.desc: Acknowledges reception of a data segment.

items.label: XFER_REFUSE
items.desc: The transmission of the current bundle is to be stopped.

items.label: SESS_TERM
items.desc: One entity wants to cleanly terminate the session.

items.label: MSG_REJECT
items.desc: Rejects a message the peer could not handle.

items.label: SESS_INIT
items.desc: Carries the session parameter inputs of one entity.
